segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How would you say the situation in Spanish?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: La situación.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. -ión is a feminine ending, so the word takes "la" for "the". La situación. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now in Spanish, adjectives, describing words, adjectives are words that describe, like "big" or "yellow" or "happy", words that we can put "is" in front of are adjectives, describing words, these words come after the noun they describe in Spanish.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So instead of saying "the global situation", for example, you say "the situation global".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: There's a bit of flexibility for emphasis as well, but the normal standard position is to come after the noun. So how would you say the global situation?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: La situación global.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. La situación global. How would you say digital camera? Digital camera.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Cámara digital.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Yeah, cámara digital. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Cámara is feminine, so a digital camera is una cámara digital. So we have "la" for "the" and "una" for "a".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how would you say: I want to buy a digital camera. What was the verb to buy?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Comprar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So: I want to buy a digital camera?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Quiero comprar una cámara digital.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Quiero comprar una cámara digital. How would you say: I want to buy the digital camera?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Quiero comprar la cámara digital.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Quiero comprar la cámara digital. What if you wanted to say: I want to buy it, and with the "it" you meant the digital camera?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Quiero comprarla.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So this "la" is "it". There's a lot of words in Spanish for car depending on where you are. It's one of the words that changes a lot between the dialects, but I think everybody understands all of the words that are heard.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: You might hear "coche", which is related to coach; "carro", which of course is car, carro, so we have two r's in carro, that's why we have this rolling r. You might hear "auto".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Where do you think auto comes from?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Automobile.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Of course, and it exists, "automóvil", but people would say "auto".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: You might even hear "máquina", which means machine. So machine, the car, máquina.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: This is another example of the q-u spelling producing k sound: m-a-q-u-i-n-a, máquina.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Máquina.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So there's a few words there for car and you might hear others as well.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Coche is masculine. So how would you say the car?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: El coche.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. "A" for masculine words is "un", u-n, un. So a car?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Un coche.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. The machine, does máquina look masculine or feminine?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Feminine.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So the machine?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: La máquina.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: La máquina. A machine?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Una máquina.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. And does carro look masculine or feminine?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Masculine.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So the car?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: El carro.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: El carro. A car?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Un carro.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Un carro. Good. So it's the noun that has the gender, not the object. Of course, it's not the car that is masculine or feminine, it's the noun, it's the word itself. So even though all of these words refer to car, some are masculine and some are feminine.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Big in Spanish is grande, grande. Of course, we can relate this to grand in English, grande.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So using any of these words that you like, how would you say the big car?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: La máquina grande.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. La máquina grande. So la máquina grande, el auto grande.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Now if you say the big cars, this adjective is also going to become plural.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: How do you say the house?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: La casa.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. And how was the houses?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Las casas.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So "la" also became plural. So las casas. If you say the big houses, big is also going to become plural.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Grandes.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how would you say the big houses?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Las casas grandes.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Las casas grandes. The big car using auto?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: El auto grande.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. El auto grande. The cars using auto, so a masculine word, you say los autos. So "el" becomes "los" in plural.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So how would you say the big cars?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Los autos grandes.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Los autos grandes. Los carros grandes. Good.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: If you want to say can you see the big car, you can say can you see or in Spanish you can just say do you see. We kind of overuse this "can" a lot in English. So: do you see the big car?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: You informal?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Mhm.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ¿Ves el coche grande?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. You needed some time there to look at "ves", and this was the more common way actually of saying in Spanish: ¿Ves el auto grande?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: But if you didn't have that time to think about it, even though it's more natural to say it like this, it really doesn't matter, you could say "can you see". Now you would probably be quicker at building "can you see" than "you see" because "can" is something very common that you're going to be using all the time.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So in conversation where you just want to get the meaning across, you might want to use this. So how would you say can you see the big car?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: ¿Puedes ver el coche grande?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So puedo, quiero, tengo que, debo, these verbs that are followed by "to" versions that you're going to be using a lot, even though the sentence is longer, they are shortcuts. They are shortcuts in thought.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And once you become very confident with that, you're going to start noticing that people say things differently to you. So instead of "I can't find it", "I don't find it", ah? You will notice that yourself and your speech will adjust, but at the beginning what you're trying to do is to be conversational and correct structurally.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Once you get over that hurdle of being communicative, you're going to start noticing that people say things differently to you, so instead of "I can't find it", "I don't find it".

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So you could say "I can't find it". How would you say I can't find it? What was to find or to encounter?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Encontrar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Encontrar. So say: I can't find it.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No puedo encontrarlo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. No puedo encontrarlo. This would be the shortcut. Even though it's longer, it's much easier to build "no puedo encontrarlo" because "puedo" is something you're going to be using all the time and then "encontrar" is in the "to" form, ah?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: I don't find it, how would that be?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: No lo encuentro.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: No lo encuentro. Good. So it's very useful to bear in mind these verbs like puedo, debo, which we can use with "to" forms, which give us a a shortcut and allow us to get conversational very quickly.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: What was to remain?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Quedar. Good. And I remain myself is how we get the meaning of I stay. So how do you say I stay?

segments.speaker: Student

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: I remain myself. I remain, myself. What's to remain?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Quedar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And what's I remain?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Aha. What's I remain myself?

segments.text: I was thinking, okay, the "me" should go first, but it can't go first because the verb is in the "to" form, and I I I I just got stuck. [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Where do you start when you're building the sentence? With the verb, with who is doing that. So if you start with that, then it's not in the "to" form anymore, ah?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So the order of thought is very important. The verb is the backbone. That's the first place we want to go. Quedo, I remain myself, me quedo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So me quedo is I stay. The word for red in Spanish is rojo, rojo. This is spelled r-o-j-o, and j's in Spanish are pronounced "kh" like this: rojo.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Rojo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: And we have the initial r, so if you can do it, it will be the rolling r: rojo.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Rojo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. So how would you say I'm staying in the red car? I'm staying in the car red. The word for in is en, e-n.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: So let's divide it up: I'm staying, only think about that bit, I'm staying, I remain myself?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Me quedo.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: In?

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: En.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: The red car, the car red, and let's use the word "auto" for car for now. So: I'm staying in the red car, the car red?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Good. Me quedo en el auto rojo. Good. How would you say I have stayed in the red car? I have stayed, I have remained myself in the red car. Again, we want to divide it up: I have remained myself. There's a lot to think about there in that first bit.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Aha. In the red car?

segments.text: Good. How would you say I have bought a red car? What is the verb to buy?

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Comprar.

segments.speaker: Student
segments.text: Comprar.

segments.speaker: Teacher
segments.text: Comprar. So: I have bought a red car, and let's use auto. I have bought a red car?

segments.text: Good. He comprado un, masculine word, un, un auto rojo. How would you say I have bought myself a red car?
